title: Product Management is Still All About Telling Stories | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: An a16z consumer partner and former LinkedIn/Twitter PM argues that AI has collapsed the cost of building software but not the cost of judgment, inverting the product loop from spec-then-build to build-then-design, so the scarce skill becomes curation and storytelling. He offers concrete diagnostics — purpose/core actions/cycle, direct traffic plus core-action retention, and Twitter's multi-step 'Learn Flow' onboarding — for telling whether a product is really being used.

themes.theme: Story, not spec, is the PM deliverable

insights.claim: Reid Hoffman's LinkedIn interview question — what artifact does a product manager produce, when engineers produce code, BD produces signed contracts and designers produce visuals — frames product management as a discipline that must justify its own output.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: A fast test for evaluating PM talent in a portfolio company or a hire: can they name and defend the artifact they actually produce?
insights.quote: “So, you want to be a product manager. What is the artifact that a product manager produces?”
insights.locator: The interview question I’ll never forget

insights.claim: The author says the spec answer he gave in that interview was wrong: a 120-page spec written for LinkedIn's jobs-inside-a-social-network product was not the most important artifact — the story was.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Diligence signal: teams whose core document is a requirements spec rather than a shared narrative are running a Waterfall-era operating model.
insights.locator: The evolution from spec to story

insights.claim: A product story must clear two bars that a specification never had to: it must be immediately understandable to whoever you are talking to, and repeatable by others faithfully without the author in the room.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Test it live — ask three people at a company to describe the product; divergence predicts scattered roadmaps.
insights.locator: The spec describes a system, what it must do

insights.claim: The whole of product management compresses to one sentence — a product manager helps their team and company ship the right product to their users — in which 'helps' explicitly means the PM is not the leader.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Watch for PM orgs positioned as mini-CEOs; the author's model says the role is leverage, not authority.
insights.quote: “A product manager helps their team (and company) ship the right product to their users.”
insights.locator: Ten years ago I gave a talk about product management

insights.claim: The author notes that a product management talk he gave ten years ago is still circulated, which he reads as possible evidence that the field has not moved.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Suggests durable, slow-changing best practice in PM craft — an area where tooling startups face a conservative buyer.
insights.locator: Ten years ago I gave a talk about product management

insights.claim: The cost of making software has collapsed by an order of magnitude, but the cost of judgment about what to build has not changed at all.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Value migrates from engineering throughput to taste and curation; price companies on decision quality, not shipping velocity.
insights.quote: But the cost of judgment hasn’t changed at all. Figuring out what to build is more important now than ever.
insights.locator: What is changing

insights.claim: Legacy product rituals — scoping, costing, arguing, up-front specs — were invented specifically to protect scarce engineering time from bad decisions, in a world where a team got only six or eight turns around the build loop per year.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: If the constraint those rituals protected is gone, the rituals are pure overhead — a concrete source of operating leverage in portfolio companies.
insights.quote: These are all rituals that we invented in order to protect engineering time from bad decisions. Because you only got six or eight turns around that loop a year.
insights.locator: Product development is a loop

insights.claim: The product loop has been reordered rather than removed: build it quickly with AI first, play with it, then design it in both the visual/UX and engineering senses, then ship and learn.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: A diagnostic for team modernity — teams still sequencing spec-then-scope-then-build are running the pre-AI order.
insights.quote: It completely inverts: from spec-and-scope, to build-and-play.
insights.locator: The old loop went: idea, spec, costing

insights.claim: The author claims this inversion from spec-and-scope to build-and-play changes product management more than anything else currently happening in the field.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Tooling that serves prototype-first workflows should compound faster than tooling built around spec documents.
insights.locator: It completely inverts

insights.claim: Prototypes beat what-ifs every time, because playing with a working artifact reveals how it feels and fits in a way argument cannot.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Ask founders how many working prototypes they built before committing a roadmap; low counts now signal wasted optionality.
insights.quote: Prototypes beat “what-ifs”, every time.
insights.locator: First, take the idea and you build it quickly with AI

themes.theme: The opposite mistake: cheap demos, expensive products

insights.claim: Demos have become almost free while working products have not, and the distance from prototype to something real still takes real time to cross.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Discount impressive AI demos in diligence; the prototype-to-production gap is where capital and time still go.
insights.quote: Demos are almost free now. Working products are not.
insights.locator: But I want to be careful

insights.claim: With coding agents available to everyone, the roadmap question shifts from a resourcing debate to an impact debate — 'this or that' rather than 'this or nothing.'
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Teams that still argue about schedule capacity are answering a question that no longer binds; watch for that as a stale-management tell.
insights.quote: It is an impact debate. “This or that”, not “this or nothing.”
insights.locator: We all have great ideas, and now we all have agents

insights.claim: The author's biggest worry about AI in product is that faster building lets teams cram everything in, producing a product-level analogue of 'AI slop' that he says he has already seen happen in a few places.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Feature bloat becomes the dominant failure mode of AI-era products; retention and coherence, not shipping counts, are the metrics to monitor.
insights.quote: We talk about “AI slop” in content; this is what AI slop means for product.
insights.locator: My biggest worry about AI

insights.claim: When anyone can build anything, deciding what to build becomes the entire job, and that decision is fundamentally a story problem about what narrative should live in customers' heads.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Curation and taste become the defensible skill in an era of commoditized building — a hiring and moat consideration.
insights.quote: When anyone can build anything, deciding what to build is the whole job.
insights.locator: My biggest worry about AI

insights.claim: The traditional PM question of whether a feature fits in the schedule should be discarded entirely in favor of whether it fits in the product.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: A one-question audit of a product review meeting: which of the two questions dominates the room.
insights.quote: The most important question is: Does it fit in the product?
insights.locator: There’s a bit of a trope about product managers

themes.theme: Vision framework: purpose, core actions, cycle

insights.claim: A product vision is distinct from a mission statement and decomposes into three parts: purpose (why someone puts the product in their life), core actions (what they actually do), and cycle (the expected frequency of each core action).
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: A portable diligence template — ask any founder for all three and note which they cannot answer.
insights.locator: What isn’t changing

insights.claim: LinkedIn's purpose was 'find and be found,' and for many users the core action was simply responding when someone reached out — a cycle of once or twice a year rather than daily.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Low-frequency products can still be enormously valuable; DAU-style benchmarks misprice networks whose core action is rare.
insights.locator: LinkedIn’s purpose was to find and be found

insights.claim: LinkedIn deliberately did not prod users into daily actions despite being a social network, instead investing enormous early effort in keeping profiles accurate so that rare inbound contact would land well.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Counter-example to engagement-maximizing playbooks: matching product mechanics to the real cycle can beat forcing frequency.
insights.locator: LinkedIn was a social network, after all

insights.claim: A team that cannot define its product's core actions does not have a product, because it does not understand what it has built.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Use as a pass/fail gate in early-stage meetings before any metric discussion.
insights.quote: If you can’t define what those core actions are, then you do not have a product, because you don’t have something that you understand.
insights.locator: If you can’t define what those core actions are

themes.theme: Measuring whether people really use it

insights.claim: Founders asked whether people use their product habitually answer with proxy metrics — a 50% DAU/MAU ratio, 10,000 signups, a million people on a waitlist, a million in ARR, four billion tokens a day, number three on the App Store — none of which answer the question asked.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Treat these headline numbers as deflections; the token-count metric in particular is an AI-era vanity stat to probe behind.
insights.locator: My whole career, as I’ve met with founders

insights.claim: The usage measurement that matters is direct traffic — people who opened the installed app icon or typed the domain by hand — counted only when they perform a core action, not merely open the app.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: A specific metric to request in diligence that strips out paid, notification-driven and re-engagement traffic.
insights.locator: Focus on direct traffic

insights.claim: On Discord the qualifying core action would be getting into a live session and actually reading and sending messages, not opening the app.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: A concrete template for defining the engagement threshold in any community or messaging product.
insights.locator: And then only really count the people

insights.claim: AI products where users type or prompt hand teams a literal transcript of the user journey, showing the exact moment a user gave up and rephrased and what they expected the product to do but it did not.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: A structurally new research asset unique to AI-native products — an underrated advantage over pre-AI incumbents.
insights.quote: You can see the exact moment someone gave up and rephrased.
insights.locator: Now, one thing that’s new, and that I love

insights.claim: The author insists those user transcripts must be read directly rather than summarized by AI, because forming the opinion about what the story is remains the human job.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Cuts against a popular 'AI summarizes your user research' product category; a warning on where automation destroys value.
insights.quote: READ THESE! AI is great for surfacing things you wouldn’t have seen before, but you can’t have it summarize everything, and you can’t have it form your opinion for you.
insights.locator: READ THESE!

insights.claim: Onboarding is the single most important moment to tell a product's story because the user will never give the product that much attention again.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Underinvestment in onboarding is a recoverable, high-ROI fix inside portfolio companies.
insights.quote: You will never get this much attention from them ever again.
insights.locator: Onboarding

insights.claim: New users split into eagers, fly-bys and a large fuzzy middle, and the middle — curious people who showed up for a reason — is the only group worth designing for, since eagers convert anyway and everyone who works at the company lives in eager-land.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Explains why internal dogfooding systematically misjudges onboarding quality — an endemic bias to correct for.
insights.quote: if you work at the company, you live in eager-land
insights.locator: You have to remember, at this point

insights.claim: More simple onboarding steps beat fewer complex ones, a result the author says he has proven in A/B tests at multiple companies over the years, with discrete simple steps beating single large screens every time.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Contradicts the common 'reduce friction by minimizing steps' instinct; a cheap, testable lever on activation.
insights.quote: More simple steps beat fewer complex ones. I’ve proven this in A/B tests at multiple companies over the years.
insights.locator: Assume your users are motivated and curious

insights.claim: AI products have made onboarding harder rather than easier, because the blank prompt box is a magic box that can do anything and therefore teaches the user nothing.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Identifies a shared, unsolved weakness across chat-first AI apps — whoever solves capability teaching wins activation.
insights.quote: You get the blank prompt box. In some ways it’s the worst onboarding screen ever designed.
insights.locator: AI products have made this harder, not easier

insights.claim: The fix for AI onboarding is teaching capabilities concept by concept with concrete examples and getting the user to at least one valuable use case quickly, ideally using their own data, rather than opening with 'Hi, I'm here to help, ask me anything!'
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: A concrete checklist for auditing any AI app's first-run experience before or after investing.
insights.locator: A lot of products nowadays start with

insights.claim: Longer onboarding flows do cause more drop-off, but the people who complete them are far more likely to actually use the product, so A/B tests should be judged on next-day and next-week return and core-action rates rather than completion of the flow.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: A measurement error that systematically pushes teams toward shorter, worse onboarding; check which metric a company optimizes.
insights.quote: Your retention data, from this point forward, is your report card.
insights.locator: People ask me sometimes: with a longer flow

insights.claim: A working onboarding can be validated by asking users at the end what the product is and checking whether they give roughly the right answer.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: A cheap qualitative test any operator can run this week, no instrumentation required.
insights.locator: If you ask them, at that moment

themes.theme: Twitter case study: the Learn Flow

insights.claim: Twitter's problem when the author joined in late 2009 was not really growth — millions signed up because the product was constantly in the news — but that nobody who signed up could say what Twitter was, so they never came back.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Top-of-funnel awareness can mask a comprehension failure; separate acquisition from activation when reading viral growth curves.
insights.quote: The problem was that no one could tell you what Twitter was.
insights.locator: A story from Twitter

insights.claim: Twitter's original onboarding offered 'Find your friends' or 'Follow 20 random people,' which most users skipped, landing them on a big empty compose box that produced the reaction 'I don't have anything to say' and then exit.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: The empty-state failure mode maps directly onto today's blank AI prompt box — the same mistake in a new medium.
insights.locator: The way we were doing onboarding was

insights.claim: The Learn Flow that Twitter rebuilt over a couple of years taught the product one concept at a time — welcome framing, what a tweet is at 140 characters, then clicking follow on the left so tweets appeared on the right to demonstrate the timeline — and moved retention more than anything else shipped that year.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: The highest-leverage retention intervention at a famous consumer company was onboarding pedagogy, not features — a reusable playbook.
insights.quote: And it moved retention more than anything else we shipped that year.
insights.locator: So we rebuilt onboarding over a couple of years

insights.claim: The closing prescription is to use AI to go faster on prototypes while refusing to speed up or surrender judgment, because defaulting to 'let's test it and see' is how teams end up with a sloppy product.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: The hardest ongoing tension — creativity versus abundant data — is where product quality differentiation now lives.
insights.quote: Use AI to go faster on the prototypes — but don’t speed up your judgment.
insights.locator: The right product for your users
